title: From 6% to 30%: Women Directors Rise in Latin American Horror and Fantasy, But Barriers Remain
summary: The landscape of genre filmmaking—horror, fantasy, and sci-fi—is undergoing a dramatic shift in Latin America, driven by a new wave of women directors. At the Costa Rica Media Market, Monica Garcia, director general of the Sitges Film Festival, announced that since the launch of the WomanInFan initiative six years ago, the percentage of female genre directors at the festival has leaped from a mere 6% to approximately 30%. "We're waiting for the next Issa López," Garcia said, referring to the acclaimed Mexican director of "Tigers Are Not Afraid." But the path remains steep. Garcia screened a documentary she directed, featuring interviews with women in the field, including Katharina Kubrick, daughter of Stanley Kubrick. "The common denominator is the difficulties," Garcia noted. "Even Katharina talks about the marginalization she suffered for being Kubrick's daughter and a woman. It's not a generational thing—it has transcended decades." The panel, which included Morbido CEO Pablo Guisa and Mexican director Luis Javier Henaine, explored the unique strengths of Latin American genre cinema. Guisa highlighted the region's shared Judeo-Christian imagination—saints, demons, and miracles—as "perfect fuel" for fantasy. He cited the legacy of Guillermo del Toro and the impact of Argentina's Blood Window program, which boosted international co-productions. Garcia pointed to the historic win of Demián Rugna's "When Evil Lurks" at Sitges in 2023 as a milestone for Latin American horror. Henaine, whose film "Disappear Completely" was hailed by Guisa as Mexico's best horror in two decades, emphasized an emotion-first approach. "I don't start by asking how to make it scary or funny. I start with the human emotion. If the situation feels real, the fear or humor follows." Despite the progress, continuity is a challenge. "Continuity is difficult for any filmmaker—and even more so for women," Garcia said. "But we've followed these talents from their first films, and they know this festival will always be waiting for them." The launch of WomanInFan LatAm aims to nurture this growing talent pool, ensuring that the next generation of female genre directors not only emerges but thrives.
why_it_matters: Representation in film shapes what stories are told and who gets to tell them. As more women direct genre movies, audiences see new perspectives on fear, fantasy, and culture, which can challenge stereotypes and inspire young people from all backgrounds to pursue filmmaking.

background_read: The Sitges Film Festival, held annually in Spain, is one of the most prestigious fantasy and horror film festivals worldwide. Its WomanInFan program, launched six years ago, aims to increase female representation in genre filmmaking.
Latin America has a rich tradition in horror and fantasy, with directors like Guillermo del Toro (who won Oscars for 'The Shape of Water') achieving global acclaim.
The Blood Window program, started by Argentina's INCAA film agency, has been instrumental in boosting international co-productions and visibility for Latin American genre films.

Despite progress, women directors still face barriers, including marginalization and difficulty maintaining career continuity, as highlighted in a documentary featuring Katharina Kubrick, daughter of legendary filmmaker Stanley Kubrick.
The new WomanInFan LatAm initiative seeks to nurture emerging talent, echoing broader global movements for gender equality in the film industry.

perspectives.description: The growth to 30% female directors marks real progress and shows that targeted initiatives like WomanInFan can make a difference. It brings fresh voices and diverse stories to horror and fantasy, enriching the entire genre.

Despite the increase, the industry still struggles with deep-rooted bias and marginalization. Women directors often find it harder to get second projects, and continuity remains a serious problem that numbers alone don't fix.

Latin American genre cinema draws on a unique cultural reservoir of religious symbols and folklore. The rise of women directors coincides with a global push for diversity, but whether this momentum translates into lasting structural change remains an open question.

WomanInFan LatAm could create a pipeline for emerging talent, but it will need sustained funding and industry support. The next step is ensuring that female directors move from shorts and festival hits to leading major international co-productions.
